doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

title: Saxophone tone and great reed sections
summary: Ware laments that young players do not strive for tone and recalls the Ellington and Lunceford reed sections.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: He wanted. It would be just perfect because Duke could see Johnny playing an idea of his. Paul Gonzalves is another beautiful saxophonist. Ben Webster, Coleman Hawkins, Don Byas. I'm talking about saxophonists. You don't find them like that no more and it's funny because those guys -- I remember Ben made a statement that his whole idea when he was coming up was to play with a beautiful tone, you know, and it seems like kids have thrown that away. They don't strive for no sound, no pure sound. Most of them, they're so busy being so technical and everybody wanted to play fast, true, but you lose something in playing fast. You don't have no tone qualities. Some of them out there know how to use it, but not like in my day coming up.
Now, I'm saying that, look like I'm a diehard, because music moves on. It's true. But I love beautiful sounds. I love beautiful sounds. I was listening recently to a whole old

Duke Ellington 1940s band, the reeds section of Hodges, Otto Hardwick, Ben Webster, Harry Carney, Barney Bigard, -- to me, that was one of the greatest reed sections in the world. Then there was Jimmy Lunceford's That was (unintelligible) reed section. Another terrible reed section -- But, Thad and eh, but bad and Mel's reed section, very beautiful. It has been. But I don't know, like you say, where music is heading. It's hard to say. I'm going to go back a little bit.
